slides.title: Observability, cost, and monitoring
slides.subtitle: By the end of this module: every run is traced, every dollar attributed, and the two biggest cost levers applied — the LO7 promise, cashed in with real numbers.
slides.notes: State the governing principle before anything else, close to verbatim: an agent can be wrong while running perfectly — no exception, no crash, just a bad decision or a quietly climbing bill. Say this is where M1's promise, 'every transition is inspectable', finally gets real numbers attached to it.

slides.title: You cannot manage an agent by testing alone
slides.intro: Non-determinism means the eval suite tells you what should happen; production tells you what actually did — and only one of those is watched continuously.

slides.title: The two big levers

cards.title: Caching
cards.body: Identical inputs should not be recomputed. Cache retrieval and deterministic reasoning keyed by input hash — a hit costs microseconds and zero tokens. Never cache anything time-sensitive without a scoped, versioned key.

cards.title: Model routing
cards.body: Send the confident, simple majority to a cheap model; reserve the frontier model for the genuine hard tail. A deterministic rule decides the tier — routing itself must never cost a token.

slides.notes: Both levers were introduced conceptually earlier in the week — M2's pattern choice, M4's stale-memory lesson, M7's deterministic routing. Say plainly: nothing here is new theory, it is old lessons finally paying a cost dividend. Two minutes before the funnel diagram.

slides.title: Three levers, compounding
slides.caption: Each lever shrinks what the next one has to work on — flow engineering removed model calls for rule-shaped work; caching removes repeats; routing cheapens whatever is genuinely left.
slides.notes: Say the order out loud and explain why it is an order: you cannot route or cache a call that flow engineering already deleted. This is the module's own diagram — the funnel of savings — rendered as a flow slide instead of a stacked bar.

slides.title: Latency and reliability signals
slides.intro: Cost is not the only signal — track and alert on the shape of the run, not just its price.

bullets.text: The customer's felt experience — a 20-second agent has failed regardless of correctness.
A rising rate flags a degrading backend before a person notices anything is wrong.
Climbing escalations mean the agent is resolving less — a quality regression, not a volume shift.
A spike may signal an attack campaign, or a broken flow that never used to trip it.
Runs creeping toward the budget ceiling warn of looping before it becomes a runaway.

slides.notes: Ask the room which of these five they would notice first in their own systems today — most will say cost, almost nobody will say step distribution. That gap is exactly why it belongs on the list; a looping agent is expensive well before anyone graphs the cost.

slides.title: Tracing: degrade gracefully, never vanish
slides.code:
# src/rafeeq/observability/tracing.py
"""Rafeeq is already a state machine (M1) -- every transition is a
traceable event. LocalTracer persists EVERY run locally; @traceable
ALSO streams to LangSmith when installed -- degrade gracefully,
never vanish, when a vendor SDK is absent."""

def traceable(run_type="chain", name=None):
    def decorator(fn):
        span_name = name or fn.__name__
        target = fn
        if LANGSMITH_AVAILABLE:
            from langsmith import traceable as _ls_traceable
            target = _ls_traceable(run_type=run_type, name=span_name)(fn)

        @functools.wraps(fn)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            with start_span(span_name, run_type=run_type) as span:
                result = target(*args, **kwargs)
                _attach_result_metrics(span, result)
                return result
        return wrapper
    return decorator

callouts.text: The LocalTracer span always fires — a participant with no LangSmith key still gets a real trace tree to read.

callouts.lead: No code change at the call site
callouts.text: langsmith.traceable wraps the SAME call when the package is installed; the decorator's caller never knows which.
M1's state machine already made every step a discrete event — this decorator just exposes it.

slides.notes: Point at LANGSMITH_AVAILABLE and ask why a course built for a classroom with unreliable network access would insist on this branch. The answer is docs/OFFLINE_MODE.md's own promise: every lab produces a trace even fully offline. Run render_tree() live if the environment is up.

slides.title: The two levers, in code
slides.code:
# src/rafeeq/observability/optimise.py
"""Cache repeats; route simple work to a cheap model. Key includes
the POLICY VERSION and LOCALE -- a cache never serves a stale
policy (the M4 lesson, cashed in here)."""

def cached_policy(question, locale, version=CURRENT_POLICY_VERSION):
    key = (_question_key(question), locale, version)
    cached = _policy_cache.get(key)
    if cached is not None:
        POLICY_CACHE_STATS.record_hit(usd_saved=_ASSUMED_RETRIEVAL_USD)
        return cached
    POLICY_CACHE_STATS.record_miss()
    result = policy_context(question, locale)   # KB retrieval
    _policy_cache[key] = result
    return result

def route_model(intent, confidence):
    # Confident, simple intents -> cheap model; the hard tail -> frontier.
    if intent in {"order_status", "track"} and confidence >= 0.8:
        return get_cheap_model()          # majority of traffic
    return get_frontier_model()           # reserved for genuine difficulty

callouts.lead: Version + locale are IN the key
callouts.text: A key on the question alone serves a stale or wrong-language policy the moment either changes.

callouts.lead: A rule, not a model call
callouts.text: route_model decides in plain Python — routing must never itself cost a token.
A policy version bump changes every key at once — no TTL clock to get wrong.

slides.notes: This is the module's code-review exercise made visible: ask the room what breaks if `version` and `locale` were dropped from the key. Someone should say 'a French — or Arabic — customer gets the English policy cached under someone else's question' before you confirm it.

slides.title: Bounded retry, idempotent tools only

callouts.text: For a write tool the retry loop does not exist in the control flow at all — nothing to misconfigure.
Never a second, hand-maintained list — retry safety reuses the read/write split you already built.

callouts.lead: RetryLedger proves it, not the source
callouts.text: ledger.assert_never_retried("issue_refund") reads the ledger back — a fact, not a re-read-and-hope.

slides.notes: Say the double-refund incident by name and ask who remembers it from M1/M3 — this is the same failure, reintroduced by a well-meaning reliability feature. Point at line one of the write branch: no try/except exists there at all, on purpose. That is the safety property, not an optimisation.

slides.statement: You cannot optimise what you cannot attribute.
slides.statement_ar: لا يمكنك تحسين ما لا تستطيع نسبته إلى سببه.
slides.notes: Say it, pause, let it land — same rhythm as every module statement this week. Connect it backward to M1's promise and forward to the next slide: a mistake caught here becomes a common-mistakes list, then a case study, then a lab that fixes it.

slides.title: Six ways observability gets skipped

bullets.text: Debugging non-determinism by re-running and hoping.
Un-actionable — attribute it, or it stays a mystery.
No version or locale in the key — stale-answer bugs, the M4 lesson again.
Duplicated money movements — the double-refund incident reborn.
Quality and cost drift silently while the error graph stays flat.
p95 is a first-class SLO, not an afterthought.

slides.notes: Cold-call each mistake before revealing its text. Ask which one the room has personally shipped — this is the module where honest hands tend to go up, because every item here looks reasonable in the moment it was written and only expensive months later.

slides.title: The 68% bill hiding in plain sight
slides.scenario: A support platform knew its agent was "too expensive" but not why. It had no tracing — debugging meant re-running and guessing. Roughly 20,000 contacts a day; the bill was double forecast, threatening the project's renewal.
slides.challenge: Finance wanted a defensible per-intent cost model before re-approving spend. Find where the money went and cut it without regressing quality — fast, and provably.
slides.solution: Tracing revealed the truth in an afternoon: 68% of spend was routine order-status contacts, each running the supervisor plus a specialist on the frontier model and re-embedding the same KB query every time. Three fixes — route order-status to the cheap model, cache KB retrieval, skip the supervisor for high-confidence single-domain intents — cut blended cost 58-61% with no measurable quality drop, provable on the eval replay.
questions: Why is one cost number un-actionable, and what does attribution unlock?
Which lever — cache, routing, or flow — would you apply first, and how would you decide?
How do you guarantee the cheaper model didn't quietly reduce quality?
What SLOs and alerts stop the bill from silently drifting back up?
slides.notes: This is the package's own case study — real numbers, not a hypothetical. Ten minutes, facilitate rather than lecture. Push on question 3: the room should name the eval-set success check specifically, not just say 'test it', before you move on.

slides.title: Lab 9 — Trace and cost Rafeeq
slides.objective: Instrument Rafeeq with tracing, produce a cost/latency report attributing spend by model and component, then cut cost with caching and model routing and add a bounded retry.
slides.setup: Lab 8 hardened Rafeeq; tickets_eval.jsonl; git checkout lab9-start

tasks.text: Add tracing; run 30 mixed tickets; open the trace tree for one refund run and identify the most expensive span.
Build the cost report: attribute total spend by model and by component; identify the single biggest cost bar.
Add KB-retrieval caching (scoped, versioned key) and model routing (cheap model for confident order-status). Re-run the 30 tickets.
Add a bounded retry for a flaky read tool; confirm the write tool, issue_refund, is never retried.
Fill BENCHMARKS.md: cost/contact and p95 latency before vs after; assert eval-set success did not regress. Commit.

slides.title: The LangSmith operating principle
slides.caption: Every production failure becomes a regression test. A change that regresses beyond tolerance never reaches main — red_team_gate and eval_harness_gate sit in the same pipeline as the unit tests, not beside it.
slides.notes: Say the SPEC line close to verbatim: LangSmith traces feed back into eval datasets, so failures become regression tests. Name evaluations/harness.py's --baseline/--gate pair and audit.replay(ticket_id) as the offline, dependency-free version of the same idea — a production incident replays into a new scenario, never just a bug fix.

slides.title: Reading fluently is not acting correctly
slides.intro: SPEC's own warning, restated as a benchmark design principle: an oracle checks a concrete effect, never the model's prose.

bullets.lead: Tone is not a pass/fail criterion.
bullets.text: "The reply sounds apologetic and helpful" scores nothing in TawseelBench — it never was the bar.
A refund above REFUND_LIMIT_SAR was never issued; a cross-customer id never appeared in a tool call.
oracle(scenario, final_state, transcript, tool_calls, store_diff) -> passed, detail. Nothing else.
An oracle whose trigger a scenario never sets still returns passed with a reason — checked, not never-checked.

slides.notes: Ask the room to name a real system they have seen graded on tone rather than outcome — most rooms can. τ-bench and its successor established the alternative shape; name it now, the next slide shows how TawseelBench applies it to Tawseel's domain.

The instructor hands you a fresh injection payload — not from the corpus.
Open a real run, attribute its spend, name the biggest bar.
forget_customer run live — zero vectors and checkpoints remain, proven on the spot.

slides.notes: Four beats, six minutes — say the timing constraint out loud, teams that overrun on beat one lose beat four. Rehearse this order with any team that asks; it is the order the instructor guide's own demo script follows, beat for beat.

slides.title: Grading is evidence-first, demo second
slides.intro: The system testifies to its own quality — traces, the security report, and CI's red-team history are read before a single slide of the demo.

bullets.text: A crisp demo cannot rescue a red CI history — the repository's own record is read first.
A fresh injection payload, not from the corpus — the instructor confirms the over-limit refund is structurally blocked.
forget_customer run on a real seeded customer — zero vectors and checkpoints, confirmed on the spot.
The academic-integrity check: matching red-team payloads or benchmark figures across repositories.

slides.notes: Name both live spot-checks explicitly before the demo block starts — teams should expect them, not be surprised. This is not a gotcha; announcing it in advance is what makes the check about the system, not about catching someone unprepared.

slides.title: Grade weighting
slides.footnote: From the assessment package's own weighting table — unchanged all week, cashed in fully on Friday.
slides.notes: This table was shown once on Monday; show it again now so the room sees the whole week converge on one number. Point at the 40% and say plainly: nothing said today changes that weight, it only changes whether the room is ready to earn it.

slides.title: PA-1 and PA-2, the two dry runs
slides.intro: The capstone's two graded artefacts were rehearsed earlier in the week — Friday is not the first time either skill is tested.

bullets.text: A broken agent — unbounded loop, a raising tool, no metadata filter — fixed and verified. 40/40/20 split.
The graded security artefact: red-team your own Rafeeq, produce SECURITY_REPORT.md, fix every high-severity finding.
Triage correctness 50%, mitigation quality 30%, governance reasoning 20% — not just 'did you find bugs'.
The deployed, traced, red-teamed Rafeeq — 40% of the course grade, evidence-first.

slides.notes: This is a recap, not new material — say so plainly, thirty seconds per bullet. The point of restating it here is that PA-1 and PA-2 are not separate from the capstone; they are its dress rehearsals, graded on the exact same skills.

slides.title: Flagship Expert badge criteria

items.text: labs + PA-1/PA-2 + quiz + capstone, combined
the rubric score on its own, not averaged away by other components
every high-severity red-team finding closed and retested held
cross-customer memory leakage = 0, checked live

slides.notes: All four must hold at once — a strong overall score cannot buy back one open high-severity finding, and a clean security report cannot buy back a red leakage test. Say this is a conjunction, not an average, before anyone asks.

slides.title: Four flags that cap a criterion at 70%

bullets.lead: A rule or authorisation living only in a prompt.
bullets.text: No branch, no server check — just a sentence a crafted message can argue with.

bullets.lead: A leakage test absent or red.
bullets.text: The cross-customer test either was never run, or was run and failed.

bullets.lead: A cost cut that regressed eval success.
bullets.text: Cheaper and worse is not a win — the exact failure this course spent a module warning against.

bullets.lead: A write tool with a retry wrapper.
bullets.text: The double-refund incident, reintroduced on purpose or by accident — either way, a hard cap.

slides.notes: These four are the assessment package's own instructor notes, verbatim in spirit. Say plainly: hitting any one of these caps that criterion regardless of everything else on the page — a beautiful architecture slide does not buy back a prompt-only refund rule.

slides.title: One system, five days, done
slides.subtitle: Nine components, nine labs, one Rafeeq — assembled, traced, red-teamed, and running in the simulated Tawseel environment.
slides.notes: Fifteen minutes, per the instructor guide's own wrap-up allocation. Slow down here — this is the section participants remember. Do not rush the through-line slide to save time elsewhere; if something has to be cut today, it was not this.

slides.title: Rafeeq, assembled from nine parts
rows: Bounded core loop, typed state, global budget
Governed tools over MCP, server-side authorisation
Thread memory, scoped long-term recall, PDPL erasure
Business rules as deterministic flow gates
Layered guardrails, red-team suite in CI
Tracing, cost attribution, caching, routing, retries
slides.notes: Read this top to bottom slowly — it is the whole course on one slide. Ask the room to point at the row they are proudest of, and the row that gave them the most trouble; both answers are worth hearing out loud before moving on.

slides.title: The through-line, named once
slides.intro: Every recurring enemy this week — a swallowed error, a stale memory, a lost handoff, a rule living in a prompt, a loop with no ceiling — was the same disease.

bullets.text: An agent can run perfectly and still be wrong — no exception, no crash, no red dashboard.
A typed state, a branch instead of a sentence, a server-side check instead of an instruction.
A step budget, a handoff budget, a cost cap — termination as a property you can prove.
A trace tree, a cost report, an SLO alert — the sense organs this week finally gave the system.

slides.notes: This is the single most important slide of the course — say the disease/cure framing slowly, and let the silence after 'silent wrongness' sit for a beat. Ask the room to name, from memory, which module gave them each cure; most will get structure and loops instantly and pause on observation, which is the point of doing M9 last.

slides.title: What comes after Friday

bullets.text: Secures this exact system further — the same Rafeeq, a deeper adversary.
Productionises it — the same Rafeeq, a real deployment target.
A reusable SDAIA Academy benchmark for later agentic AI programmes, not a one-off lab artefact.
As much structure as possible, as much agency as necessary — it does not expire with the course.

slides.notes: Name both follow-on course codes clearly and say what each one assumes: a working Rafeeq, not a fresh start. This is the moment to tell anyone who is proud of a capstone extension that it is not wasted work — the next course builds on exactly that repository.

slides.title: What the instructor collects

items.text: full history, every checkpoint commit
LangSmith project or reports/traces/
signed off, zero open high-severity
real measured numbers, not the package's illustrative ones
issued within five working days of submission

slides.notes: Read this out as the literal collection list at the end of H5 — do not let anyone leave the room before the instructor has all five links. State the five-working-day figure explicitly so participants know when to expect their result.

slides.statement: An agent that cannot show its work is not ready to act on your behalf.
slides.statement_ar: الوكيل الذي لا يستطيع أن يُظهر عمله ليس جاهزًا للتصرف نيابةً عنك.
slides.notes: Say it, pause, let it land — the last statement of the course, same rhythm as every one before it. This sentence is deliberately the M1 premise and the M9 promise fused into one line: acting requires structure, and structure is only real if it can be shown.

slides.title: Day 5 in one line
points: You cannot optimise what you cannot attribute — and now you can attribute everything.
Rafeeq is not a demo; it is nine components that testify to their own quality.
The maxim held from Monday to Friday: as much structure as possible, as much agency as necessary.
Go build the next one — with the sense organs already switched on.
slides.notes: Close the course on this slide, no further content after it. Thank the room, confirm the badge-collection checklist is complete for every team, and point once more at the two forward-pointer course codes before dismissing the cohort for good, on time.
